title: Telnet Option Specifications
summary: Specifies the general form for Telnet options and how they are described. It replaces RFC 651 and is an Internet Standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Telnet, the remote-terminal protocol, can be extended with options such as larger displays or different character sets. RFC 855 sets the rules for those extensions: one person assigns each option a unique code, and every option is written up in a fixed five-part format. It also explains how two hosts trade option settings before they exchange the details.

questions: how are telnet option codes assigned
subtitle: How Telnet options get their codes and how each option has to be documented.

tldr.problem: Telnet options let hosts handle dissimilar devices better than the basic Network Virtual Terminal allows, but option codes must not collide and options need clear documentation.
tldr.mechanism: One named person assigns option codes, each option is documented in five standard sections, and a two-step subnegotiation using WILL, DO, SB and SE exchanges option parameters.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard. Documentation is generally required before a code is assigned, though it may be waived for some experiments.

today: RFC 855 is an Internet Standard. No later RFC obsoletes or updates it, and it remains the specification for documenting Telnet options.

sections.title: Purpose of Telnet Options
sections.content:
The point of options in the TELNET Protocol is to let hosts find more elegant solutions to communication between dissimilar devices than the Network Virtual Terminal (NVT) framework allows. Hosts should be able to invent, test or discard options at will, but options that prove generally useful are expected to be supported by many hosts, so they should be carefully documented and well publicized. It is also necessary to make sure one option code is never used for several different options.

This document specifies a method of option code assignment and standards for documentation of options. The person responsible for assigning codes may waive the documentation requirement for some cases of experimentation, but in general documentation is required before a code is assigned. Options are publicized by publishing their documentation as RFCs. The RFC names Jonathan B. Postel at USC-ISI as the assigner.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet can grow new features. To keep the growth orderly, every feature gets one unique code, and the feature is written up and published before it is widely used.

sections.title: Documentation Sections
sections.content: Documentation of an option should contain at least five sections. Command Name and Option Code names the option and its code. Command Meanings describes the meaning of each TELNET command relevant to the option; complex options that need subnegotiation may have more commands. Default Specification states the default assumptions for hosts that do not implement or use the option. Motivation explains why the option, or its particular form, was invented. Description (or Implementation Rules) furnishes a fuller account, such as text, a sample implementation or hints to implementers, because command meanings and motivation alone do not always ensure that two implementations can communicate.
sections.plainLanguage: Every option write-up names the option and its code, explains each command, states what non-participants should assume, gives the reason it exists, and adds enough detail for two independent implementations to work together.

sections.title: Subnegotiation
sections.content:
Some options need more information than a single option code, for example an option that carries a parameter. The strategy has two steps. First the parties agree to discuss the parameters: one party proposes the option with DO (or WILL) followed by the option code, and the other accepts by returning WILL (or DO) followed by the option code. Once both parties agree, subnegotiation runs with SB, the option code, the parameters, and SE. For an option called ABC the commands are IAC WILL ABC, IAC DO ABC and IAC SB ABC <parameters> IAC SE.

Each party is presumed able to parse the parameters, since each has said the option is supported. Even so, a receiver may find the end of a parameter string by searching for the SE command (IAC SE) if it cannot parse the parameters. Either party may end subnegotiation at any time by sending WON'T or DON'T.

Designers of options that use subnegotiation must take great care to avoid unending loops. If each party accepts any parameter value and both propose different values, acknowledgments may oscillate forever, each side believing it is only acknowledging the other's new proposal. If a parameter byte has the value 255, it must be doubled, following the general TELNET rules.
sections.plainLanguage: First the two sides agree to discuss a setting with simple yes-or-no commands. Then they trade the actual values between start and end markers. Designers must make sure this exchange always finishes.
